reset: Reset puts the original settings.json back.
title: Right-size Spark for three teams: starter pool, custom pool, autoscale and high concurrency
objective_text: Choose the default pool, a custom pool's node size and scaling, and session sharing so three teams each get the Spark compute their work needs.
scenario: One workspace serves analysts, a nightly ETL job and data scientists. Someone made a big fixed pool the default for everyone: analysts now wait minutes for a session, and the ETL pool is both too small per node and too big on quiet nights.
engine_label: A model of a workspace's compute pool settings, checked on this PC
verifies: Your pool settings give each team what its work needs, as the Spark compute pages describe pools, node sizes, autoscale and high concurrency, checked against a model on this PC.
does_not_verify: That any pool is created or any session starts: nothing runs here.
Capacity limits, such as the Spark vCores a capacity allows and the 200-node pool limit.
The exact conditions under which notebooks share a high concurrency session.

expected.description: Default Starter pool (Medium); NightlyETL Large, autoscale 2 to 12, dynamic allocation; high concurrency on; Analysts and DataScience on the starter pool.

validation.fail: Interactive sessions won't start in seconds.
validation.pass: Analysts start fast on the starter pool.

rules.why: A custom pool as the default makes sessions take about three minutes to start.
Starter pools support only Medium nodes; another size means on-demand startup of 2 to 5 minutes.

validation.fail: The nightly pool doesn't fit the job.
validation.pass: NightlyETL has 16-vCore nodes and scales between 2 and 12.

rules.why: Large nodes have 16 vCores and 128 GB.
With autoscale the pool scales between its minimum and maximum nodes and retires them after the job.
Dynamic allocation lets the job request more executors when tasks exceed what it has.

validation.fail: Notebooks can't share a session, or the wrong role creates pools.
validation.pass: Notebooks share sessions, and only workspace Admins create pools.

rules.why: High concurrency mode lets users share a single Spark session across several notebooks.
Creating a custom pool needs the Admin role in the workspace.

hints: Which pool starts in seconds, and what makes it slow?
What lets one pool grow on busy nights and shrink on quiet ones?
explanation: The starter pool keeps Medium-node sessions ready, so they start in seconds; a different node size, or a custom pool as the default, means minutes. A custom pool fits a heavy job: Large nodes give 16 vCores, autoscale moves between a minimum and maximum, and dynamic allocation adds executors as tasks need them. High concurrency lets notebooks share one session. Only workspace Admins create custom pools.
review_notes: Checked on Learn 2026-11-06: spark-compute (starter pools start in 5-10 seconds, Medium only, other sizes mean on-demand startup of 2-5 minutes; custom pools take about three minutes; node sizes), create-custom-spark-pools (Admin role; autoscale between min and max; dynamic executor allocation), workspace-admin-settings (high concurrency shares a Spark session across notebooks).
